## Source
https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/carbon-dioxide/ and Our World in Data — CO₂ and Greenhouse Gas Emissions (Global Carbon Budget 2025)

## Atmospheric CO₂ Concentration

The latest measurement from NOAA's Mauna Loa Observatory (February 2026) records atmospheric CO₂ at **429 parts per million (ppm)**. This represents a more than 50% increase from the pre-industrial baseline of approximately 280 ppm. The current level is at least 1.5 times greater than the natural increase observed at the end of the last ice age 20,000 years ago — a change that took thousands of years then but has occurred in roughly two centuries now. Ground-based and satellite measurements confirm the sharp acceleration, linked primarily to the burning of coal, oil, and natural gas.

## Global Emissions Trajectory (1750–2024)

Before the Industrial Revolution, CO₂ emissions were negligible. Growth remained relatively slow until the mid-20th century. In **1950**, the world emitted roughly **6 billion tonnes** of CO₂. By **1990**, emissions had nearly quadrupled to over **20 billion tonnes**. Today, global annual emissions from fossil fuels and industry exceed **35 billion tonnes**. While emissions growth has slowed in recent years, they have not yet peaked.

![Annual CO₂ emissions by country](./assets/figure_3.jpg)

## Who Emits the Most? Country-Level Totals

China is the world's largest emitter by a significant margin, producing over 12 billion tonnes annually — more than one-quarter of the global total. The United States peaked near 6 billion tonnes around 2005 and has since declined to roughly 5 billion tonnes. India has risen rapidly to approximately 3 billion tonnes. Europe's share has fallen substantially.

| Country / Region | Approx. Annual CO₂ (billion t) | Share of Global | Trend (recent) |
|---|---|---|---|
| China | ~12.5 | ~27% | Slight increase |
| United States | ~5.0 | ~14% | Declining |
| India | ~3.0 | ~8% | Rising |
| EU-27 | ~2.7 | ~7% | Declining |
| Germany | ~0.6 | ~1.7% | Declining |
| United Kingdom | ~0.3 | ~0.9% | Declining |
| Brazil | ~0.5 | ~1.4% | Roughly stable |
| France | ~0.3 | ~0.8% | Declining |

In 1900, Europe and the US accounted for more than 90% of global emissions. By 1950, they still represented over 85%. Today, they account for less than one-third, while Asia — home to nearly 60% of the world's population — produces roughly half of all emissions. Africa and South America each contribute only 3–4%, comparable to international aviation and shipping combined.

## Per Capita Emissions: Extreme Inequalities

Per capita CO₂ emissions reveal stark global inequalities. The world's highest per capita emitters are major oil-producing nations with small populations (Qatar, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait). Among large, populous countries, the US, Australia, and Canada have per capita emissions roughly three times the global average.

![Per capita CO₂ emissions over time](./assets/figure_1.jpg)

| Country | Per Capita CO₂ (tonnes/year) |
|---|---|
| United States | ~15 |
| Canada | ~13 |
| Australia | ~15 |
| South Africa | ~8 |
| China | ~9 |
| EU-27 | ~7 |
| World average | ~5 |
| United Kingdom | ~4 |
| France | ~4 |
| India | ~2 |
| Kenya | <1 |
| Chad / Niger | ~0.1 |

The gap between the highest and lowest per capita emitters is approximately **150-fold**: the average American or Australian emits in under two days what the average person in Chad or Niger emits in an entire year. Importantly, countries with similar living standards can differ significantly — France and the UK have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of their energy mix (higher nuclear and renewable shares).

The 2024 map of annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions shows a mixed picture. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines (roughly −1% to −5%), shown in blue. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations saw increases of +2% to +10% or more, shown in orange and red. Some countries in South America (notably one or two) experienced very large percentage increases (>10%), while others saw declines.

![Annual percentage change in CO₂ emissions, 2024](./assets/figure_4.jpg)

- **Global CO₂ emissions now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year** and have not yet peaked, despite slowing growth rates.
- **China alone accounts for over 25% of global emissions** (~12.5 Bt), more than double the United States (~5 Bt); India (~3 Bt) is the third-largest and rising fast.

# Slide 01 - Global CO₂ Emissions: Trends, Regional Shifts, and Per Capita Inequalities

This briefing examines CO₂ emissions from the Industrial Revolution through 2024, connecting total emissions growth, regional shifts, national responsibility, per capita inequality, and the role of energy mix. The evidence base is NASA, Our World in Data, and the Global Carbon Budget 2025.

# Slide 02 - Atmospheric CO₂ Reaches 429 ppm — 50% Above Pre-Industrial Levels

The latest Mauna Loa measurement cited in the source brief is 429 ppm in February 2026. That is more than 50% above the pre-industrial baseline of about 280 ppm. The key point for negotiators is speed: a change that occurred over thousands of years at the end of the last ice age has been compressed into roughly two centuries, driven primarily by burning coal, oil, and natural gas.

# Slide 03 - Global Fossil Fuel CO₂ Emissions Grew Six-Fold: 6 Billion to 35+ Billion Tonnes

Global fossil fuel and industrial CO₂ emissions were negligible before the Industrial Revolution, rose to roughly 6 billion tonnes by 1950, exceeded 20 billion tonnes by 1990, and now exceed 35 billion tonnes per year. Growth has slowed, but the source brief is explicit that emissions have not yet peaked.

# Slide 04 - China Now Emits Over 12 Billion Tonnes — More Than Double the United States

Country totals show a highly concentrated emissions landscape. China emits about 12.5 billion tonnes annually, or roughly 27% of the global total. The United States emits about 5 billion tonnes, about 14%, after peaking near 6 billion tonnes around 2005. India is third at about 3 billion tonnes and rising fast, while the EU-27 is declining at about 2.7 billion tonnes.

# Slide 05 - Asia Now Accounts for ~50% of Global Emissions; US + Europe Below One-Third

The geography of emissions has changed dramatically. In 1900, Europe and the United States accounted for more than 90% of global emissions; by 1950 they still represented more than 85%. Today, Asia produces roughly half of global emissions, while the United States and Europe together are below one-third. Africa and South America each contribute only about 3–4%.

# Slide 06 - Per Capita Gap: 15 t in the US vs. 0.1 t in Chad — a 150× Disparity

Per capita emissions reveal inequalities hidden by national totals. The United States is about 15 tonnes per person per year, Canada about 13, China about 9, EU-27 about 7, the world average about 5, the United Kingdom about 4, India about 2, Kenya below 1, and Chad or Niger about 0.1. The high-to-low gap is approximately 150-fold.

# Slide 07 - 2024 Snapshot: US and Europe Cut Emissions While Russia and SE Asia Increase

The 2024 annual percentage change map shows a mixed picture. The United States and much of Europe recorded declines of roughly 1% to 5%. Russia, parts of Southeast Asia, and several African nations increased by about 2% to 10% or more. Some South American countries saw very large percentage increases above 10%, while others declined.

# Slide 08 - Energy Mix Explains Why France Emits Far Less Per Capita Than Germany

The source brief highlights that prosperity alone does not determine per capita emissions. Countries with similar living standards can have significantly different outcomes depending on energy mix. France and the United Kingdom have much lower per capita emissions than Germany or the Netherlands, largely because of higher nuclear and renewable shares versus higher fossil fuel shares.

# Slide 09 - Key Takeaways: Emissions Are Still Rising, But the Map of Responsibility Is Shifting

The synthesis is fivefold: global emissions exceed 35 billion tonnes and have not peaked; China alone accounts for more than one-quarter of global emissions; the geographic center has shifted toward Asia; per capita inequality remains extreme at roughly 150 times; and policy choices, especially energy mix, shape per capita emissions outcomes.
EOF
